entry.title: ALIENS NEOPLASMA - A brilliant ZX Spectrum game appears on the Amstrad Plus via AI/Devil System
entry.content:
The Amstrad CPC Plus has just received a new release with unofficial port of Aliens NeoPlasma, a tense horror platformer developed by Devil System with the help of AI. Originally released to high acclaim on the ZX Spectrum by the Sanchez Crew, this atmospheric title tasks players with guiding protagonist Ashley Smith after she awakens aboard the starship Achilles. What was meant to be a routine journey quickly devolves into a desperate fight for survival. Players must navigate a treacherous labyrinth of ladders, platforms, and automatic doors, managing scarce resources like ammunition and grenades while searching for the safety of a medical bay.


▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

This new enhanced version takes full advantage of the Amstrad Plus hardware to deliver a pretty decent effort. The gameplay itself utilizes the system's high-resolution MODE 1 graphics, which are further elevated by custom sprite colours and hardware-accelerated ASIC sprites that hope to ensure smooth, fluid action on screen. While the actual gameplay leans into this sharper display mode, the game's atmospheric cover and title screen still utilize the more colourful MODE 0. Players will need to use every terminal and counter they can find to survive the terrors lurking in the dark corridors of the ship—assuming they can stay alive long enough to reach them.

entry.title: Insector X - An unofficial AI fan port of Taito's 1989 horizontal shooter by caiusarcade {WIP}
entry.content:
Caiusarcade has just released an early build of an unofficial fan port of Taito's 1989 horizontal shooter Insector X for the Commodore Amiga. Rather than building a remake from the ground up, this  conversion uses static recompilation to translate the original arcade machine's dual Z80 processors straight into native 68020 code. Every piece of game logic, artwork, and audio is pulled straight from the coin-op original, with the developer and the full use of AI assistance verifying the translated code frame by frame and matching the Amiga display pixel by pixel against the arcade release.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

To get this arcade-accurate insect blaster running, you will need an Amiga 1200 (or another AGA based machine) equipped with a hard drive, Kickstart 3.x, around 1.3 MB of free chip RAM, and at least 4 MB of fast RAM, though 8 MB is ideal. While a stock 14 MHz 68020 keeps the gameplay and music running at full speed with a lower refresh rate during hectic moments, stepping up to a 50 MHz 68030 or faster delivers faster performance throughout most of the action. Setting up the game is also straightforward if you have the ROMS, as users can compile the build using a simple one-click tool on Windows 10 or 11, or put it together on Linux and macOS using Python 3 and vasm.

- Please note the Audio seems to be broken in the video which may be early beta related

entry.title: AcidBoutique - A new music tool for the Commodore Amiga, a 303 bassline synth and a 808 drum machine!
entry.content:
On the topic of music and not retro gaming, here's a new piece of software called AcidBoutique, a  music production tool for the Commodore Amiga created by solo developer wintermute303. Built in the developer's spare time with the help of AI, this software squeezes the authentic sound and feel of two iconic electronic instruments—the TB-303 bassline synthesiser and the TR-808 drum machine—onto a classic 40-year-old Amiga 500 with just 1 MB of RAM or more. Instead of relying on rough approximations, the software is the result of reverse-engineering, running the genuine logic of the original hardware in real time on the Amiga's Motorola 68000 processor so that every slide, accent, and drum hit behaves just like the real deal.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

It is the kind of studio setup bedroom producers would've probably liked to have had back in the 1990s. Because of copyright restrictions however, Amiga users will need to supply their own original 303 and 808 ROMs to get started, with full instructions tucked inside the manual. Priced at roughly the cost of a single cup of coffee, wintermute303 is offering the tool to the community in hopes that a little support will help fund future updates for this music development tool.

  • Thanks to Rochabian and thedaemon letting me know, you can find MAME tr303.zip and tr808.zip by googling it.

entry.title: Blue Max: Megadrive Remake - A fan remake of Blue Max, the 1983 World War I flight game!
entry.content:
Here's a new Sega Mega Drive game, it's the 'Blue Max: Megadrive Remake', a homebrew project from developer gerla.cc. Drawing direct inspiration from Peter Adams’ Commodore 64 port of Bob Polin’s 1983 World War I classic, this version preserves the original game's core world and mechanics while giving them a modernized megadrive overhaul. Players are put back in the cockpit of a classic biplane, soaring over rivers, roads, and bridges to bomb enemy tanks, ships, and buildings while dogfighting rival aircraft. Between bombing runs on the enemy city, you will need to touch down on friendly airfields to refuel, repair damage, and restock your ammunition as you work your way up from a lowly Kamikaze Trainee to the prestigious rank of Blue Max.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

To take full advantage of the Mega Drive and Genesis, gerla.cc rebuilt the game from the ground up to run at a smooth 60 frames per second, introducing a fresh perspective alongside visuals rendered directly from 3D models. The remake also offers plenty of flexibility for both newcomers and seasoned veterans of the 1983 original, featuring three distinct difficulty tiers—Beginner, Advanced, and Expert. Additionally, players can tailor the flight physics to their liking by toggling gravity on or off and switching between Normal and Pilot control schemes, making it easier than ever to jump right in and have a blast.

entry.title: Aonic - HOT NEWS as Sonic the Hedgehog gets an early v2 demo on the Amiga and it's impressive! [UPDATE]
entry.content:
Well this is incredible news, and one I didn't expect for a bank holiday Monday. As a classic gaming icon has made a surprising leap over to the Commodore Amiga 1200 as a highly anticipated work-in-progress demo of Sonic the Hedgehog. Titled as Aonic and released by reassembler, this impressive technical feat ports the blue spinning hedgehog over from the Sega Mega Drive to the Amiga. This project over the many months of development, has captured the attention of Amiga retro gamers eager to see how Sega's flagship title performs on the Commodore A1200 hardware.

The underlying engine relies directly on the original Mega Drive source code, utilizing the comprehensive disassembly published by the Sonic Retro team. Because it shares this foundational DNA, the homebrew port plays identically to its console counterpart, preserving the precise physics, momentum, and speed that defined the 1991 classic. However, because the remainder of the game is still being implemented, certain aspects of the performance and design could still improve or degrade before a final release.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

NEW DEMO GAMEPLAY WITH AUDIO SOON


Translating the game to the Amiga required significant engineering adjustments because the two systems are very different pieces of kit, despite sharing a similar 68000-based CPU. Specifically, hardware like the Amiga 1200 struggles with bus contention when moving large amounts of data around—a hurdle that is easy to circumvent when designing an Amiga game from scratch, but highly problematic when porting an existing title at high quality. To overcome this, the rendering engine was heavily optimized and rewritten for the Amiga, resulting in some necessary visual differences while keeping the gameplay intact. You can see all the deviations from the Megadrive Version (HERE)


[UPDATE] Reassembler has officially released the second playable demo for Aonic (Sonic The Hedgehog). This latest version brings the ambitious port closer to a finished game by adding full music and sound effects. The release follows a thorough round of hardware testing that successfully cleaned up several performance bugs. Developer reassembler also credited artist Ric for providing valuable help with the project's visual artwork. Work is already moving fast on the next stages of the game. Creating the initial Green Hill Zone took the developer about 12 months of difficult groundwork. However, progress on the upcoming Marble Zone is moving much quicker. This new level will only take about four weeks to port. The faster timeline is possible because the custom optimization tools built during the first year of development are fully reusable.

entry.title: Death Mask 3D - Apache Software Amiga FPS using using a first-person 3D engine
entry.content:
CodyJarrett has made available another update for Death Mask 3D, a technical overhaul of Apache Software’s classic Amiga title. While the original game relied on a grid-based, step-by-step movement style reminiscent of Dungeon Master, this updated iteration transforms the experience into a true first-person shooter akin to Wolfenstein 3D. Built with the assistance of the Claude AI model, the new project renders all 34 original campaign missions and 10 multiplayer arenas in a fluid, continuous 3D engine. It preserves the authentic atmosphere of the source material by retaining the original wall textures, enemy sprites, weapon graphics, HUD layout, and sound design. Amiga owners dive into the full single-player campaign—complete with its authentic mission briefings, passwords, and cinematic intro and ending screens—or jump into split-screen mode for two-player co-op or deathmatch battles.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

Latest source has a newer version

Developed for any Amiga 1200 or above, the game moves away from the original title's support for older A500 machines, requiring at least a 68020 processor, Kickstart 3.0, and 2MB of Chip RAM. Interestingly, advanced AGA chipsets are not necessary, as the visual presentation uses a 32-colour palette with the copper coprocessor handling the vibrant sky, floor, and lighting gradients. CodyJarrett has packed the release with quality-of-life enhancements, including optional Fast RAM optimization for a smoother frame rate, a native Workbench icon, and a live HUD automap that toggles with the press of a key. To ensure the game runs smoothly across different hardware configurations, players can choose between three distinct graphical detail levels or use CD32 joypad support to map strafing to the shoulder buttons. For those who simply wish to explore the nostalgic environments without the pressure of combat, built-in cheat keys are also included.

entry.title: Sword - A Polish Amiga Classic That Deserved Better (Amigaguru Guest Review)
entry.content:
Sword, developed by Serio Comic, was their second (and possibly final) game, and it clearly showed how much they had learned since their debut game Gate 2 Freedom which was also a platformer. The game delivers plenty of replay value, backed by a consistent visual style and cohesive level design throughout. Every stage introduces enough new ideas and challenges to keep you coming back for more.

One feature that initially annoyed me was the strict time limit, but it also introduced something I've never seen before or since. When you die, you restart at the beginning of the level, but every enemy you've killed and every item you've collected remains gone. Even better, the timer is frozen until you reach the point where you originally died. This removes much of the frustration usually associated with retracing your steps, and because you already know where many of the traps and tricky jumps are, progression still feels natural even after repeated deaths.

A Challenge, Lots Of Bosses, A Timer And A Gun...

Sword throws plenty of challenges your way, yet your only means of defence is a fairly weak gun with one of the strangest sound effects I've ever heard in a game. You get used to it over time, but I still wish there had been weapon upgrades or additional health boosts to make combat a little more rewarding.

The levels vary considerably in both length and difficulty. Some can feel quite drawn out because your weapon is so weak, forcing you to spend a lot of time clearing enemies and obstacles. There are also a few light puzzle elements scattered throughout the game, but thankfully they never disrupt the pacing. As most of my readers know by now, I generally dislike puzzles in platform and action games, yet Sword never pushed me to that breaking point. In fact, I've completed it at least three times over the last three decades. Sword is far from a new game; it originally launched in 1998 and was one of the final commercial releases for the Amiga 500 before receiving a revival many years later.

One of the aspects that impressed me at launch, and still does today, is just how technically accomplished the game is. There's plenty of parallax scrolling, huge bosses, fantastic music and sound effects running simultaneously, responsive controls, and excellent pacing across a large variety of levels and locations. The game even includes an auto-scrolling snowboarding bonus stage, something you almost never saw on the Amiga at the time. While the main character sprite isn't particularly remarkable, it's important to remember that this is an Amiga 500 title requiring just 1MB of RAM and spread across four floppy disks. Considering those limitations, Sword makes outstanding use of the hardware and puts many older, and even some newer, Amiga games to shame.


This One Fell Between Two Worlds...

This was also the last title from Titan Computer published for the classic Amiga OCS/ECS hardware. Afterwards, the company published several ground breaking PowerPC releases for the platform, including Shogoand Heretic II (which I worked on for Hyperion, by the way). That makes Sword something of a swansong for the ECS and AGA era. There were several ambitious projects planned afterwards, such as Evil's Doom and Alien Nations, but unfortunately most of them disappeared into development hell and never saw release.

Sword sold poorly, likely due to a combination of being a Polish production and receiving a very limited print run. As a result, boxed copies are now considered quite rare, even if that rarity isn't reflected on sites such as Hall of Light or Lemon Amiga. Of course, it didn't help that the game arrived during the height of the original PlayStation era, when flashy 3D games dominated the market. Back then, many of us wanted the Amiga to follow the same path rather than continue producing what looked like "simple" 2D games.

Ironically, looking back today, it's the 2D titles that have aged gracefully. Most early 3D games now look rough at best, while quality pixel art remains as appealing as ever. Sword still looks fantastic today, just like other great 2D classics from the era such as The Misadventures of Lomax and Hercules on the PlayStation.

The Box & The Stuff Inside...

Sword - The Breathtaking Game (as it says on the floppy labels) might not come with the most impressive packaging or packed-in extras, but it certainly features some of the most unusual box art of its era. Not my favourite at launch, but the artwork gradually grew on me over the following decade. I did take photos of the back of the box, but they didn't turn out particularly well due to just how much information (and the amount of color crash/mix) is crammed onto it. If you're interested in seeing it, I can always take another shot, but for now you can simply head over to Hall of Light and check out my box scan there.

The included manual is printed entirely in black and white, and the floppy disk labels follow the same budget-friendly approach. Considering the state of the Amiga market at the time, that's perfectly understandable. Amiga games were struggling commercially, and publishers were understandably reluctant to spend heavily on packaging and presentation for products that might never sell enough copies to justify the investment.

Summary...

A really solid game that was overlooked and forgotten by many Amiga fans. Had it been released six years earlier, it could easily have been a major hit because all the ingredients for success are here. That's exactly why I've added it to my long-running TGWNTABS series, which now stands at a whopping 24 articles dedicated to games that you absolutely need to play before deciding that only modern games are worth your time.

Whatever way you get hold of it, do yourself a favour and give Sword a try. It remains one of the finest late-era Amiga platform shooters, and it deserves far more recognition than it ever received. If you enjoy it, spread the word, leave a comment online, and help ensure this forgotten classic continues to shine.

As mentioned, Sword is a fairly rare Commodore Amiga 500 release, meaning you'll most likely need to track it down through abandonware archives or other preservation sources. Finding a boxed copy today is incredibly difficult, although with more and more collectors selling off their collections these days, you never know. It's a little sad to see, if I'm being honest. 

Guest article by AmigaGuru

entry.title: The Rescue - A new action game for the C64 by Fernando64JJ

entry.title: Icy Escort - A route-planning Platformer released by Donut 80 for the C64
entry.content:
Welcome to the latest game called Icy Escort, a brand-new Commodore 64 title developed by Donut 80. In this charming puzzle-platformer, players guide a dedicated mother penguin on a race against time to gather her missing chicks before the clock strikes midnight. Each snowy stage requires players to scout the treacherous wintry landscape to locate the lost babies. As each chick is successfully rescued, it tags along directly behind the mother, forming a growing line of penguins that follows her every move through the frozen wilderness.

▶ Ver vídeo en YouTube

The gameplay mechanics offer a twist on traditional movement by relying heavily on momentum and environmental rules. Players navigate the world using just a single jump button, while the penguin automatically marches forward. Changing direction is impossible on your own; instead, you must rely on strategic bounces off arrow indicators, crates, and the borders of the screen. This limitation transforms the platforming into an intricate puzzle where timing and careful path planning are essential to avoid hazards. Along the journey, players can stomp on enemies and collect ice cream treats to reset a multiplier timer and boost their high scores, though safely rescuing every single chick remains the ultimate goal.
